lead: A resistance thermometer measures temperature through resistance. The RTD (resistance temperature detector) is a coil or thin film of pure metal, usually platinum; its resistance rises steadily with temperature. The thermistor is a small bead or disc of sintered ceramic oxide; its resistance falls steeply and nonlinearly. Both are passive, so a small current is passed through them and the voltage drop is read. They serve laboratory work, process plants, air conditioners, car engines and biomedical probes.
prereq: You need: calibration, accuracy and first-order response from the sensor characteristics, and potentiometers for turning resistance into voltage.

sections.h3: The RTD: a metal resistor used as a thermometer

blocks.text: An RTD is fine platinum wire, or a thin platinum film on ceramic, with a defined resistance at 0 °C called R₀. Pt100 means R₀ = 100 Ω; Pt1000 means 1000 Ω. The larger value gives a larger voltage for the same current, and, more importantly, makes fixed lead resistance a ten times smaller fraction of the element resistance, so lead error is ten times smaller in °C.

Platinum is standard because it does not oxidise, its curve repeats from batch to batch and over years, and it is nearly linear. Nickel is more sensitive but drifts; copper is linear but oxidises above about 150 °C. Both cover narrower spans.

blocks.where: R<sub>T</sub> is resistance at temperature T (Ω); R₀ is resistance at 0 °C (Ω); α is the temperature coefficient of resistance, 0.00385 /°C for platinum; T is temperature in °C.

blocks.text: Thus a Pt100 reads 138.5 Ω at 100 °C. Sensitivity is 0.385 Ω/°C, or 0.385 %/°C. Platinum works from −200 °C to 600 °C, but over that span the line bends, so the quadratic term is needed.

blocks.where: Callendar–Van Dusen form. A = 3.9083 × 10⁻³ /°C, B = −5.775 × 10⁻⁷ /°C² and C = −4.183 × 10⁻¹² /°C⁴ for platinum; C is 0 for T ≥ 0 °C.

blocks.text: Connecting wires add resistance. A two-wire circuit measures R<sub>T</sub> + 2R<sub>L</sub>, where R<sub>L</sub> is one lead. For a Pt100, 0.385 Ω is 1 °C, so a 0.5 Ω lead pair reads about 1.3 °C high. Lead resistance also drifts with cable temperature.

A three-wire circuit uses three equal leads and cancels one lead drop against another. It works only while the leads are equal, which is true when they share a cable. A four-wire (Kelvin) circuit sends current through the outer pair and senses voltage across the inner pair. No current flows in the sense leads, so lead and contact resistance drop out. Precision Pt100 work uses four wires.

blocks.where: ΔT is temperature rise above surroundings (°C); I is measuring current (A); R<sub>T</sub> is element resistance (Ω); P<sub>D</sub> is the dissipation constant in the surroundings (W/°C).

blocks.text: That rise is self-heating. At 1 mA through 100 Ω the power is 0.1 mW; with P<sub>D</sub> = 5 mW/°C the error is 0.02 °C. In still air P<sub>D</sub> is smaller and the error grows; in stirred water it is larger. Keep current near 1 mA or less, or switch it on only for the reading.

sections.h3: The thermistor: a ceramic with a steep curve

blocks.text: A thermistor is sintered oxides of manganese, nickel, cobalt and iron, pressed into beads, discs or chips and sealed in glass or epoxy. An NTC thermistor falls in resistance as temperature rises; it is the sensing type. A PTC thermistor rises sharply beyond a transition temperature and serves as a self-regulating heater or overcurrent guard, not a thermometer.

blocks.where: T and T₀ are absolute temperatures in kelvin; R₀ is resistance at T₀ (usually 25 °C); β is a material constant in kelvin, typically 3000 K to 4000 K.
Fractional sensitivity per kelvin. At 300 K with β = 3500 K it is −3.9 %/°C, about ten times the 0.385 %/°C of a Pt100. The minus sign means resistance falls as temperature rises.

blocks.text: The gain costs range and straightness: an NTC covers about −50 °C to 150 °C and is far from linear, so even a 50 °C stretch needs a table or linearising network. The dissipation constant P<sub>D</sub> is the milliwatts that raise it 1 °C; the thermal time constant is the seconds to reach 63.2 % of a step, the first-order response of dynamic characteristics. Beads are small and fast. β and R₀ carry tolerances, so two units from one bin can differ by a degree or more.

sections.h3: Choosing between them, and biomedical probes

blocks.text: For wide span, accuracy and stability, choose Pt100 or Pt1000 with three or four leads. For a narrow span where cost, size and resolution matter more than linearity, choose an NTC and store its curve in the instrument.

Biomedical sensing uses both to about 0.1 °C. A skin or catheter probe must be small and fast, which favours an NTC bead. A reusable clinical thermometer must let tips be swapped without recalibration, which favours interchangeable thermistors or platinum. Current is held to tens of microamperes so I²R<sub>T</sub> heating stays under a hundredth of a degree.

examples.question: (a) Find the resistance of a Pt100 at 50 °C with α = 0.00385 /°C, and state sensitivity in Ω/°C and %/°C. (b) An NTC is 10 kΩ at 25 °C with β = 3500 K. Find its resistance at 37 °C and average sensitivity in %/°C over that span.
steps: Part (a). R<sub>T</sub> = R₀(1 + αT) with R₀ = 100 Ω, α = 0.00385 /°C, T = 50 °C.
Change = 19.25 Ω over 50 °C, so sensitivity = 0.385 Ω/°C = 0.385 %/°C.
Ratio = 3.04/0.385 = 7.9, about eight times. The 3.9 %/°C quoted in the text is the local sensitivity at 300 K; averaged over this 12 °C span the figure is lower, about 3.0 %/°C.
examples.answer: (a) 119.25 Ω at 50 °C, sensitivity 0.385 Ω/°C or 0.385 %/°C. (b) 6349.6 Ω (about 6.35 kΩ) at 37 °C, average sensitivity 3.04 %/°C.

examples.question: A clinical probe uses the same 10 kΩ, β = 3500 K thermistor on top of a 10 kΩ fixed resistor; the output is taken across the fixed resistor. Find the output at 35, 37 and 42 °C with a 3.3 V supply and the average sensitivity. The bead’s dissipation constant is 1 mW/°C: find the self-heating at 37 °C, and repeat with a 0.5 V supply.
steps: Thermistor values from R = R₀ exp[β(1/T − 1/T₀)]: 6832 Ω at 35 °C, 6350 Ω at 37 °C, 5309 Ω at 42 °C.
Average sensitivity = (2.156 − 1.961)/7 = 27.9 mV/°C, so a 0.1 °C step is 2.8 mV, easy to resolve.
Self-heating at 37 °C: I = 3.3/16 350 = 202 µA; P = I²R = (202 × 10⁻⁶)² × 6350 = 0.259 mW; ΔT = 0.259/1 = 0.26 °C. Too large for a 0.1 °C thermometer.
With 0.5 V: power scales with V², so P = 0.259 × (0.5/3.3)² = 5.9 µW and ΔT = 0.006 °C; the sensitivity falls to 27.9 × 0.5/3.3 = 4.2 mV/°C, still 0.42 mV per 0.1 °C.
examples.answer: 1.961, 2.018 and 2.156 V; 27.9 mV/°C at 3.3 V, but 0.26 °C of self-heating. At 0.5 V the heating is 0.006 °C and the sensitivity 4.2 mV/°C.

traps: Putting Celsius into the β equation. It needs absolute temperature; add 273.15 to both T and T₀ before you divide.
Quoting R₀ at the wrong temperature. For an RTD, R₀ is at 0 °C; for a thermistor, the quoted value is usually at 25 °C.
Forgetting the leads. In a two-wire Pt100 circuit 0.385 Ω of lead resistance is a full 1 °C of error, and the error drifts with cable temperature.
Ignoring self-heating. The element sits above the surroundings by I²R<sub>T</sub> / P<sub>D</sub>, and that error grows in still air where P<sub>D</sub> is small.

quiz.q: What does NTC stand for, and which way does an NTC thermistor’s resistance move as temperature rises?
quiz.a: Negative temperature coefficient: its resistance falls as temperature rises.

quiz.q: Why is platinum preferred over nickel and copper for RTDs?
quiz.a: Platinum does not oxidise or corrode, its characteristic repeats closely from unit to unit and stays stable over years, and its curve is nearly linear over −200 °C to 600 °C. Nickel is more sensitive per degree but drifts; copper is linear but oxidises above about 150 °C, so both are limited to narrower spans.

quiz.q: A Pt1000 has R₀ = 1000 Ω and α = 0.00385 /°C. Using the linear law, find its resistance at 80 °C and its sensitivity in Ω/°C.
An NTC thermistor is 10 kΩ at 25 °C with β = 3500 K. Find its resistance at 0 °C.
quiz.a: T = 273.15 K, T₀ = 298.15 K. 1/273.15 − 1/298.15 = 3.0697 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹; times 3500 gives 1.0744. R = 10 000 × exp(1.0744) = 29 283 Ω, about 29.3 kΩ. Resistance rises as temperature falls, as expected for an NTC.

quiz.q: A four-wire Pt100 reads correctly, but the same element on a three-wire connection shows a small residual error. Explain where the error comes from.
quiz.a: The three-wire scheme cancels lead resistance only while the leads are exactly equal. Any mismatch from different lengths, joints or temperature gradients along the cable leaves a fraction of a lead resistance in the reading. For a Pt100, 0.385 Ω is 1 °C, so even a small imbalance matters. The four-wire scheme has no current in the sense leads, so lead and contact resistance cannot enter the reading.

beyond: Not for the exam. Thin-film platinum elements are pushing RTDs smaller and faster, thermistor arrays watch every cell of an electric-vehicle battery, and printed NTC inks make flexible skin-temperature patches. Search for platinum RTD tolerance classes and thermistor interchangeability.
